title: Different Lives and Experiences
keyIdea: Children's lives can be very different. Some have a disability, some are young carers, some live in poverty, and some are new to the country and still learning the language. These are their circumstances: things they did not choose and you often can't see. What you see a child do may have a reason behind it. Judgement decides something bad about a person without knowing their story; compassion tries to understand and then does something kind, like changing a game so everyone can join in.

kid: Every child has a different life. Some live with one grown-up, and some live with lots. Some use a wheelchair. Some moved here from far away and are still learning English. These things are called circumstances. Most of them were not chosen.

You can see what a child does, but not always why. Jade yawns in class. She might be lazy, or she might help look after her mum at night. A child who helps care for someone at home is called a young carer.

Some families do not have enough money for the things most people have. This is called poverty. In the UK it is about 9 children in a class of 30. You can't tell who by looking, and it is never the child's fault.

Judgement is deciding someone is bad before you know their story. Compassion is trying to understand, then doing something kind. You can ask, 'Do you want to play?', or change a game so everyone can join in.
adult: This topic sits in PSHE Relationships education at Key Stage 2 and the IB PYP PSPE identity strand. Children learn that families and lives differ, including disability, poverty, young caring, illness and being new to the country, and that differences in circumstances call for respect and inclusion rather than judgement.

A common mistake is reading a visible behaviour as a character trait: tired means lazy, quiet means rude, old clothes mean careless. Another is believing you can tell who is poor by looking. A third is pity in place of compassion: feeling sorry from a distance, or helping without asking, which can take away a child's choice and dignity.

The facts are real. About 30% of UK children (4.3 million in 2022–23) live in relative poverty after housing costs, roughly 9 in a class of 30. Many young carers are of primary age. Families rarely tell school about either, so the safe stance is to assume there may be a reason you can't see.

In the lab your child matches behaviours to hidden reasons, swipes thoughts to judgement or compassion, compares a day with Kofi's, a young carer, tries and fails to spot poverty by looking, and changes a tag game so Nadia, who uses a wheelchair, and Yusuf, who is new to English, can join in.

familyTip: When your child says someone is 'weird' or 'lazy', ask: 'What might be going on for them that we can't see?' Then plan one kind thing together, like inviting a new child to play.

visual.caption: Judgement or compassion? Drag each thought, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: She is always late. She doesn't care.
His lunch is small. He must be greedy at home.
He talks funny, so he isn't clever.
She can't walk, so she can't be on the team.
Maybe something is hard at home. I'll be friendly.
I could show him the way to the hall.
Let's pick a game she can play too.
I'll ask if he wants to play.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the reason behind what you see, swipe judgement from compassion, live a young carer's day, and change a game so all can join.

practice.prompt: Omar hardly talks in class. He moved here from another country {n} weeks ago. What is the most likely reason?
practice.hint: Think about his circumstances. What changed for him {n} weeks ago?
practice.explain: He is still learning English. Talking in a new language is hard, so being quiet is not rudeness. You could help by smiling and using simple words.

practice.prompt: Kofi looks after his dad most evenings. His homework is late {n} times this term. What is the kind way to think?
choices: His evenings are full of caring jobs
He does not care about school
practice.hint: Kofi is a young carer. What fills his evenings?
practice.explain: His evenings are full of caring jobs, so late homework {n} times is not laziness. Calling him lazy is a judgement.

practice.prompt: A class in the UK has 30 children. About how many of them live in poverty?
practice.hint: It is about 3 in every 10 children.
practice.explain: About 9, because roughly 3 in every 10 UK children live in poverty. You can't tell which ones by looking.

practice.prompt: Nadia uses a wheelchair. Your group is playing tag on the bumpy grass. What is the best change?
choices: Play on the flat playground so she can join in
Play without her because it is easier
practice.hint: Change the game, not who is allowed to play.
practice.explain: Moving to the flat playground lets Nadia join in. Leaving her out because she is different is not fair.

choices: Trying to understand someone, then doing something kind
Feeling sorry for someone from far away
pool.hint: Compassion has two parts: understanding and doing.
pool.explain: Compassion is understanding someone's feelings and then doing something kind. Just feeling sorry from far away is pity.

pool.prompt: 'Her coat is old, so she must be messy.' What is this thought?
pool.hint: Does the thought know her story, or decide something bad about her?
pool.explain: It is a judgement. An old coat can mean her family is short of money, which is not her fault and says nothing about her.

choices: A child who helps look after someone at home
A child who has a pet
A child who is very kind at school
pool.hint: Think about Kofi and his dad.
pool.explain: A young carer is a child who helps look after someone at home, like a parent who is ill or disabled.

pool.prompt: Can you tell which children live in poverty by looking at them?
choices: No, you can't tell by looking
pool.hint: In the lab, did the guesses match?
pool.explain: No. Poverty does not show on the outside, so judging by clothes or looks is unfair and often wrong.

pool.prompt: Lily leaves school early {n} Tuesdays in a row. Which is the fair thought?
choices: There may be a reason I can't see
pool.hint: You see what she does. Do you know why?
pool.explain: There may be a reason, like a hospital check-up. Leaving early {n} Tuesdays in a row does not tell you why.

pool.prompt: Yusuf arrived from another country {n} days ago and is still learning English. How can you explain a game to him?
choices: Show the rules with your hands, and use simple words
Tell him to learn English first
pool.hint: What helps someone follow when the words are new?
pool.explain: Showing with your hands and simple words helps him follow. Louder and faster makes a new language harder.

pool.prompt: Why is it unfair to judge someone for their circumstances?
choices: They often did not choose them, and you don't know their whole story
Because circumstances are the same for everyone
pool.hint: Can a child choose to be a young carer or to be poor?
pool.explain: Children rarely choose their circumstances, and you only see a little of anyone's life. So compassion fits better than judgement.
